d.g: A form of rusk, usually sweetened bread enriched with eggs that is baked and then sliced and toasted until dry and crisp; considered easy to digest and therefore given to the ill and used as a teething food for toddlers.
d.x:
Ogden Nash, Adventures Of Isabel
She nibbled the zwieback that she always fed off,
And when it was gone, she cut the giant's head off.

zwieback.e: From German Zwieback, from zwie- (“twi-, two-”) + backen (“to bake”) (i.e. “twice-baked”), a calque of Italian biscotto (but not to be confused with it).

d.g: Swiss theologian whose sermons began the Reformation in Switzerland (1484-1531)

zwingli.e: Borrowed from German Zwingli, itself from Alemannic German Zwingli.

d.g: United States physicist who invented the iconoscope (1889-1982)
A molecule, such as an amino acid, that carries both a positive and a negative charge.

zwitterion.e: Unadapted borrowing from German Zwitterion, from Zwitter (“hermaphrodite”) + Ion (“ion”).

d.g: A two-handed sword primarily of Renaissance Germany, up to a fathom in length, invented in the 14th century.
d.x: Their major weapon was the pike, which could be up to 18 feet in length, but those whose duty it was to advance in the front line carried instead the fearsome Zweihänder; an enormous battle-sword around 66 inches in length.

Zweihänder.e: Borrowed from German Zweihänder (literally “two hander”), from zwei (“two”) + Hand (“hand”) + -er.

d.g: A zwischenzug that is a check.
A town in Masovian Voivodeship, Poland.

Zweifach.e: Borrowed from German Zweifach, a Jewish Ashkenazi surname.

d.g: A municipality of South Holland, Netherlands.
A Z letter used by Russian nationalists, usually to support Vladimir Putin or the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

zwastika.e: From Russian Z + swastika, comparing the Russian nationalist usage of the Z letter to the Nazi German swastika as a symbol of war against Ukraine. See the Russian section on Z for more information.

d.g: A type of pebble that has two curved faces formed by wind-blown sand.
Pursued after evaluating its consequences and consideration of the various means to achieve it.

zweckrational.e: From German. Used by Max Weber.
